In Fintech, Trust Is the Product and the Channel Is Whoever Already Has It.

By lowob · 14 July 2026 · Updated 10 November 2026 · 4-minute read · Revenue / Fintech

A fintech product can offer a better price and a cleaner experience than an established competitor, and still struggle to acquire customers. People are being asked to trust an unfamiliar company with their money, identity, or financial information. A good website alone doesn't settle that concern.

That is why distribution for financial products is partly a problem of trust. The question isn't only where to buy attention. It's how to help the right customer understand what the product does, who is responsible for it and why they should believe its claims.

Trust comes before traffic

For some financial services, paid channels require additional approval or verification. Rules vary with the product, country and platform. For example, Google's financial products policy includes category and location-specific restrictions, including certification for some cryptocurrency and speculative products.

But an advertising approval is only one obstacle. A potential customer may still ask: Who holds my money? What happens if something fails? Which fees apply? Can I reach someone when I have a problem? The answers should be easy to find before a user is asked to register or transfer funds.

Marketing that promises safety without explaining the protections, or highlights a return while hiding conditions, may generate attention but undermine the trust the business actually needs.

Work through people and platforms customers already use

Product and distribution partners. A payroll or accounting platform might introduce a relevant financial service to customers who already rely on its software. A wallet or marketplace could do something similar. The partner still has to believe the product is suitable for its users.

Practitioners and educators. Accountants, advisers and specialists can help explain a product's purpose and limitations. A useful walkthrough or carefully written comparison can answer questions a short ad cannot. Any paid relationship and relevant disclosures should be clear.

Owned resources. A straightforward product guide, pricing page, help center and customer emails can answer questions after someone first encounters the brand. Those channels are under the company's control, although customers still need a reason to trust what they say.

These options are not guaranteed to be cheap or simple. Partner distribution takes negotiation and integration work. A creator's audience may be poorly matched. The right channel is the one that reaches suitable customers and produces meaningful product use.

Make the proof visible before asking for commitment

Consider a hypothetical small-business payments platform. A promising introduction comes from accounting software. Before referring customers, the partner wants to understand reconciliation, failed payments, support ownership and fees. Its customers may care less about the technology than whether payments arrive on time and errors get resolved.

The useful marketing response is a clear guide to how payments work, realistic examples of the settlement process, approved descriptions of risk, and accessible support details. Those assets help both the partner and the customer make a decision.

Use the same approved facts in outreach, presentations and product pages. When the operating details change, update the material promptly.

Make compliant marketing easier to repeat

Don't treat legal and compliance review as the last obstacle before publishing. Work with the appropriate advisers to create an approved set of claims, disclosures and examples that the team and its partners can actually use.

That may include which products can be advertised in a particular market, what supporting evidence is required, how fees must be described and what disclosures a creator or affiliate needs. The specific requirements depend on the product and jurisdiction; an internal template isn't a substitute for legal review.

The benefit is practical: sales, partnerships and marketing can move faster without repeatedly improvising on sensitive claims.

Judge channels by customers, not just leads

Start with a small number of suitable channels. Ask how each will be measured. A newsletter might produce visits, a partner may introduce qualified businesses and a creator may generate sign-ups. Those actions are different distances from revenue.

For an account-based product, follow the path from qualified referral to completed onboarding, first meaningful financial action and retained use. Include referral fees, incentives and integration work in the cost. A channel producing fewer but better-qualified customers may be more valuable than one producing the most traffic.

The original argument remains: when the customer needs trust before taking action, distribution should help establish that trust rather than merely buying more impressions.

lowob takeaways

  • Lead with what customers need to verify. Explain custody, fees, risk and support clearly.
  • Choose trusted channels deliberately. Partners and practitioners help when their audience and the product actually fit.
  • Make claims review reusable. Approved language and clear disclosures make partnerships easier to operate.
  • Measure meaningful use. Track qualified onboarding and retention, not just visits or sign-ups.

Sources and notes

Google Ads, Financial products and services policy. Details category restrictions, certification and location-specific rules.

Google Ads, Financial products and services disclosures. Describes required transparency for financial advertising.

The payments-platform example is hypothetical. This article is strategic guidance, not legal advice or a report of client results.
